moments.context_summary: Carmen reviews ad copy for Love Like Wild photographer Shannon Lee. Initial drafts say 'No posing, just real moments' and 'No awkward posing.' Shannon pushes back that she does pose people (just not awkwardly), taking roughly 90% candids. They settle on 'authentic, not staged' because she doesn't stage or fake moments during the day.
moments.proposition: A single word in ad copy can misrepresent your service and repel your ideal client.
moments.audience_relevance: Photographers and other visual vendors often market a style that isn't absolute; small wording choices shape who applies and who books.
qualifications: Client-specific ad copy review, not a measured A/B test.
The final wording was a judgment call between vendor and agency, not validated against performance.
reasons: Reveals a concrete positioning correction that changes who the ad attracts.
Shows the vendor's own clarification of what she does versus what the copy implied.

moments.context_summary: Carmen sets expectations with Shannon for the Love Like Wild Google Ads launch: the first two weeks leave the ads alone and let data run, monitor for 72 hours, expect leads after about a month, and take a full 3 months (90 days) to know if it's truly working.
moments.proposition: Google Ads needs a 90-day runway before evaluation; early silence is normal, not failure.
moments.audience_relevance: Owners who stop or panic-spend after a few weeks never give search ads the data they need.
qualifications: Agency practitioner's stated process, not audited results.
Individual results vary by buyer intent and search volume.
reasons: Gives a concrete evaluation window instead of vague 'wait and see.'
Explains the sequence: no-touch period, 72-hour monitor, month-one leads, 90-day verdict.

moments.quote: 20% of people go from the page
moments.context_summary: Carmen and Fallon review a destination-wedding-planner client whose Meta ads are clear but whose landing page is vague above the fold. About 20% of visitors reach the inquiry form but don't submit. Fallon notes Meta visitors arrive with ad context; Google visitors don't, so the page must carry the explanation.
moments.proposition: When ads promise clarity, the landing page must deliver it or traffic leaks at the form.
moments.audience_relevance: Any vendor running paid search must make sure the page answers 'what do you actually do?' before asking for contact info.
qualifications: One client's observed behavior, not a controlled test.
The 20% figure is an internal estimate, not audited.
reasons: Connects a specific leak (reach form, no submit) to a specific cause (vague hero section).
Distinguishes Meta from Google traffic, which changes what the page must prove.

moments.context_summary: Fallon audits Davis and Gray Farms and finds lead volume is acceptable but roughly 55% of ad-sourced tours cancel, with reasons including destination-wedding decisions and work emergencies. She recommends narrowing targeting to closer zip codes and improving the landing page.
moments.proposition: Good lead volume can still mean a broken funnel if tours cancel at high rates.
moments.audience_relevance: Venues and planners should track tour show/cancel rates, not just inquiry counts.
qualifications: Cancellation reasons are self-reported by the client.
reasons: Shows a metric owners often ignore (tour cancellation) that undermines lead quality.
Pairs the problem with two concrete fixes: tighter targeting and page clarity.

moments.quote: there's so much noise in the emails
moments.context_summary: Fallon reports that at Views at Sunset Ridge, venue guests responded more readily to text follow-ups about tours (including cancellations and feedback) than to email. Whitney agrees text is underutilized and suggests pre-tour texts that introduce the host with a photo and directions to build rapport before arrival.
moments.proposition: Text follow-ups can outperform email for venue tour conversations.
moments.audience_relevance: Venues and planners rely on tour show rates; the follow-up channel matters.
qualifications: Internal observation from one venue account, not a controlled test.
Text response rates not measured against email in a split test.
reasons: Concrete anecdote: guests used text to cancel or give feedback on tours.
Suggests a specific pre-tour text structure, not just 'use text.'

moments.context_summary: During The Penny's messaging call, the venue already has a venue-comparison chart showing what's included in its all-inclusive package versus venue-only competitors, but it sits hidden under a FAQ dropdown and is described as 'almost too simple.' Whitney and Fallon agree it would be powerful on the ads-traffic landing page.
moments.proposition: Your strongest differentiator is useless if couples can't find it.
moments.audience_relevance: All-inclusive venues are routinely compared to venue-only rentals; the value gap must be visible, not buried.
qualifications: Client-confirmed asset exists but placement is weak; no performance data.
reasons: The value prop exists but is buried under a FAQ dropdown.
Both agency and client agree it would strengthen the paid landing page.

moments.context_summary: Whitney demos LeadLock to Zadie, a UK wedding photographer taking up to 20 weddings a year. She calls the system 'amazing' but rejects the $147/month subscription plus $12.97 setup, noting she currently pays about £20/month and her volume doesn't make the higher cost viable.
moments.proposition: A system that works for venues may not fit a small photographer's economics.
moments.audience_relevance: Owners should match tool cost to their booking volume before adopting.
qualifications: Single prospect's stated budget and volume.
Pricing is the vendor's stated offer, not a discount or current promotion.
reasons: Clear objection tied to concrete volume (20 weddings/year) and current spend (£20/month).
Client affirms product quality but rejects on economics, a common pattern.

coverage_notes: m2 contains internal onboarding and Google Tag Manager walkthrough detail but no consequential client-facing decision beyond the camcorder-rental client bidding on wrong keywords; retained as context for m4's platform-fit moment.
m5 is a non-wedding business (waxing); its Google Ads cost-per-booking and Meta-for-new-leads discussion is reported with a wedding-transfer caveat and not used as a wedding case study.
m6 is internal admin (invoices, storage, task tracking) with no interpretable buyer or growth evidence; excluded.
m7 is internal; the text-vs-email observation and sequence-refresh discussion are reported as internal-only.
m4 and m7 are internal team meetings; client names and account details are treated as internal-only sensitivity.
No measured conversion or revenue results are supplied for any client; all outcome claims are reported as observed or estimated, not audited.
